parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.guidance: All three correct scores 2 marks. Only two correct scores 1 mark.

hints: Hint 1: Think about the test for a vector - does the quantity need a direction to make sense, like displacement needs north or down as well as a size?
Hint 2: Check each one in turn - acceleration involves change of velocity, speed is just how fast, and power is rate of energy transfer with no direction.
parts.proper_answer: acceleration: vector; speed: scalar; power: scalar.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the vector-scalar test**
Think of it simply sitting beside you. A vector needs both a size and a direction to fully describe it. A scalar needs only a size. Velocity is a vector because $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ east is different from $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ north.

Step 2: **Apply to the three quantities**
Acceleration is rate of change of velocity, so it inherits direction - it is a vector. Speed is magnitude of velocity only, with no direction - it is a scalar. Power is rate of doing work, $P = W/t$, energy has no direction - it is a scalar.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A ball is projected with a horizontal velocity of $1.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from point A at the edge of a table, as shown in Fig. 1.2.

{{figure:figure_1_2}}

Fig. 1.2

The ball lands on horizontal ground at point B which is a distance of $0.43\text{ m}$ from the base of the table. Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the ball to fall from A to B.
hints: Hint 1: Focus only on the horizontal motion first - with no air resistance, what happens to the $1.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ while the ball is in the air?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate horizontal from vertical**
The great trick with projectiles is that horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontally there is no acceleration because air resistance is negligible, so horizontal velocity stays constant at $1.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Use distance = speed x time**
Horizontally: $$s_x = v_x t$$ $$t = s_x / v_x = 0.43 / 1.1 = 0.39\text{ s}$$ This same $t$ is the time of flight for the vertical fall.

enrichment.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: projectile motion independence of horizontal and vertical
uniform horizontal velocity with no air resistance
hints: Hint 1: Focus only on the horizontal motion first - with no air resistance, what happens to the $1.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ while the ball is in the air?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate horizontal from vertical**
The great trick with projectiles is that horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontally there is no acceleration because air resistance is negligible, so horizontal velocity stays constant at $1.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Use distance = speed x time**
Horizontally: $$s_x = v_x t$$ $$t = s_x / v_x = 0.43 / 1.1 = 0.39\text{ s}$$ This same $t$ is the time of flight for the vertical fall.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use your answer in (b)(i) to determine the height of the table.
hints: Hint 1: Now switch to the vertical motion - what is the initial vertical velocity when the ball just rolls off horizontally?
Hint 2: Think which SUVAT equation links vertical distance fallen, starting from rest, with acceleration $g$ and your time from (b)(i).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **List vertical quantities**
Initial vertical velocity $u_v = 0$ because projection is purely horizontal. Vertical acceleration $a = g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards. Time $t = 0.39\text{ s}$ from (b)(i).

Step 2: **Calculate vertical drop**
Use: $$s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$$ With $u = 0$: $$s_v = \frac{1}{2} \times 9.81 \times 0.39^2$$ $$s_v \approx 0.75\text{ m}$$ This is the height of the table.

hints: Hint 1: Now switch to the vertical motion - what is the initial vertical velocity when the ball just rolls off horizontally?
Hint 2: Think which SUVAT equation links vertical distance fallen, starting from rest, with acceleration $g$ and your time from (b)(i).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The ball leaves the table at time $t = 0$.

For the motion of the ball between A and B, sketch graphs on Fig. 1.3 to show the variation with time $t$ of

1. the acceleration $a$ of the ball,

2. the vertical component $s_{v}$ of the displacement of the ball from A.

Numerical values are not required.

{{figure:figure_1_3}}

Fig. 1.3

markscheme_points.text: horizontal line at a non-zero value of $a$.

hints: Hint 1: For the $a$ against $t$ graph, ask yourself what force acts after leaving the table if air resistance is negligible, and whether it changes.
Hint 2: For the $s_v$ against $t$ graph, think how vertical speed behaves - it starts at zero and gets faster, so does equal time add equal distance?
parts.proper_answer: 1. $a$-$t$: horizontal straight line at non-zero $a = g$. 2. $s_v$-$t$: curve from origin with increasing gradient.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Acceleration-time shape**
Once in flight the only force is weight, giving constant acceleration $g$ downwards. Constant means no change with time, so on $a$ against $t$ axes draw a horizontal straight line above the $t$-axis, starting at $t = 0$.

Step 2: **Vertical displacement-time shape**
Vertical velocity starts at zero and increases as $v = gt$. So the ball covers more distance each second. That means the $s_v$ against $t$ graph starts at the origin with zero gradient and curves upwards with increasing gradient - a $t^2$ parabola shape. No numbers are needed, just the correct shapes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A ball of greater mass is projected from the table with the same velocity as the ball in (b). Air resistance is still negligible.

State and explain the effect, if any, of the increased mass on the time taken for the ball to fall to the ground.

markscheme_points.text: curved line from origin with increasing gradient.
acceleration (of free fall) is unchanged / not dependent and so no effect (on time taken).

hints: Hint 1: With air resistance still negligible, think about what determines the vertical acceleration - does a heavier mass fall faster in free fall?
parts.proper_answer: No effect on time. Acceleration of free fall $g$ is independent of mass when air resistance is negligible.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why mass does not matter**
In free fall, weight $mg$ causes acceleration $a = F/m = mg/m = g$. The $m$ cancels. So a greater mass has greater weight but also greater inertia by the same factor, leaving $g$ unchanged at $9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$. With the same height and same $g$, the time to fall $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ is unchanged.
